post.caption: The Golden Gate was named before gold. In 1846, Army captain John Fremont gave the strait its name. He compared it to the harbor of Byzantium, the Golden Horn. His reason was a golden gate for trade with the Orient. That was two years before gold turned up at Sutter's Mill. So the gold in the name meant trade, with no metal involved. The name first appeared in print in his 1848 memoir. He also wrote it in Greek, as Chrysopylae. The strait is only one to three miles wide. The bridge opened in 1937, painted orange instead of gold.
